comments.text:
I got happy for no reason. I have a 1070. :-( 
At least I have SLI, not like my B-350 motherboard can support it, nor can I afford another graphics card. But I just need an excuse to be happy. In all honesty I feel like since the Crypto-currency crisis has passed prices will go down sooner or later. But all of these price hikes from Nvidia just convinces me The Vega 64 is a better value. Actually the 1080ti is also decent value once these RTX cards are released and it's price drops further. Honestly I can live without SLI, or NV-link or whatever Nvidia wants to call it. There are few people who have that kind of money, and the SLI performance is not as efficient, it makes more sense to just buy a more powerful graphics card later when it comes out. But the lack of it, just makes these prices all the more unjustifiable, because it's better to have options, and in a year later Nvidia could re-release it with the SLI component soldered on to the PCB. The only thing that could justify these prices were if these cards shipped with Free-Sync support (And we all know that's never happening), but that would cause PR nightmare for Nvidia, since the older cards technically could also get Free-Sync through a patch. Nothing justifies this kind of price hike, like when gamer focused cards are costing as much as industrial, research AI development cards, and workstation cards, (Like the Titan, and the Quadro) you know they messed up horribly. All we can do is wait for Navi to either be a (better productivity/decent gamer) card like Ryzen (making it good enough to consider), or making it so price to performance value oriented that even Nvidia will have to lower their prices. A part of me feels as if Nvidia saw how the Crypto market inflated the Vega 64's MSRP price on the secondary market, and they still assumed that Crypto would still be going big, and thought well lets just increase the prices so even if these get to a secondary market with an inflated price we'll still get more in profit. The Vega 64 was had an MSRP of $500 at launch, the online price was $1500. So when Nvidia starts selling their $700+ card for $1200 it kinda makes sense. They're no longer targeting gamers there targeting would-be Crypto miners in hopes that once the market rises again they'll cash in.

comments.text:
Lol wtf this is not even remotely true. A GTX 1080 is absolutley overkill for 1080p displays unless you're really gunning for extremely high fps in competitive games on an extremely high refresh rate monitor, like over 144hz. And even that may not warrant a 1080 given that competitive gamers will absolutely drop image settings to pump more frames. And youd also need to invest in a higher end cpu to pull this kind of thing off. To the average gamer this is just a nonsense proposition compared to upping resolution and getting the most out of their 1080.

It really just comes down to the games you're playing which determines how good a GPU you need. Modern open world AAAs specifically tend to be the outlier GPU killers where you may need to drop some settings, but just about every other type of game, even high production AAAs that just arent open world, are not nearly as demanding as the kinds of games that get cherry picked for benchmarks precisely because they're representative of the absolute worst case, pushed to the absolute limit workloads.
Just recently Linus tried to price match a PC build with an Xbox Series X and showed off that a GTX 1070 with dogshit cheap accompanying components could still handle Doom Eternal at 4k resolution at a steady 60 fps.
A 1080 is still perfectly fine for 1440p and honestly the 2070 isnt even that much faster to warrant saying that it's ok for 1440p and the 1080 isnt. And both of these GPUs are definitley more than just "ok" for 1440p resolution for that matter. Your elitist mentality is what causes so many people to overspend on their GPUs compared to what they actually need.

comments.text: The 2070 they have is in fact NOT a Founder's Edition card. However, it IS a reference card. Reference cards are different from founder's edition cards, as they are manufactured by third-party companies like MSI, Asus, or Gigabyte but still use the same cooler design as the founder's edition cards. Those companies can ALSO manufacture their own custom PCB's and coolers for the GPUs they manufacture. So, you end up with three different types of cards: Founder's Edition, Reference Cards, and Custom Third-Party Cards. Hope this helps.

comments.text:
I'm sorry guys for doing this to you.. but just a thought based on my research because I'm looking for the best VR headset.  This is only my opinion, so please feel free to discuss (BUT NO INSULTS, I'M HAPPY TO ADMIT MISTAKES, BUT THIS IS ONLY AN OPINION)... Graphic Texture X or GTX is mainly to exploit H/4K/OLED tech to the best of their abilities.  As such Ray Tracing X or RTX, is actually a technology developed for VR to exploit the 3D space.  For example, watching a Movie in 4k in 2D with depth of field means that stuff is blurry to make important bits stand out (to focus your attention).  However, that same Movie in 4k and 3D, means you dont see the burry stuff because the depth of field makes the image look 3D.
As RT (Ray Tracing) is designed to project light in multipul dimentions essentially manipulating a 3D space in a 2D environment, is it possible, to even just concider, the option; that RTX is being built on purpose for the future of VR technology.  RT is designed to improve the 3D environment.... But it will not work in a 2D world, which is why it is soo critised.  RT will not improve your screenplay, but it WILL improve your VR play.  VR is based on 3D environments, RT is based on improving the 3D space.  Its only logical to conclude, that RT wasn't desined for 2D gaming, its actually designed for 3D gaming such as VR.  The multi-dimentional lighting produced by RT will make the VR 3D gaming experience MORE real.

comments.text: On the Nvidia side: The 2070 is a great card, among the best available. Keep in mind drivers already brought improvements and will continue to do so while the pascal cards are left behind.  What resolution do you want to game at and what refresh rate, and how often would you like to upgrade are the questions that can help. 2060/1660ti may be the best choice for 1080p 60 right now, the 2070 is solid for 1440p and crushes 1080p (dont skimp on the cpu). It also provides a slightly better future proofing with the 2 GB extra vram.  The 2080 and ti variant are kings for 1440p and up but at a premium. The 2070 sits in the bastard territory, however it's not always a bad thing if you aim to keep the card a little longer. A 2060 might start showing trouble in 2 years while the 100-150 extra of the 2070 gives you an extra year or two. Buying the best you can afford at the time you need/want it isn't unreasonnable logic either (AMD cards are pretty decent  value too for 1080p saving some money for an upgrade next gen around summer 2020)

comments.text:
The story is different now in January 2019. The low prices for those GTX 1080 cards didn't last (I briefly saw some offered for under $375); they were a case of NVidia and its partners clearing out inventory of the previous generation. The few GTX 1080 cards that remain now cost as much as the RTX 2070, which happily can actually be found at the $500 list price or even less. A quick look at the featured products on a search for "RTX 2070" turned up five cards at exactly $499.99, including two that had promo codes to make the price even lower. Meanwhile, the cheapest GTX 1080 is $750, which is an utterly stupid price to pay for one when they will sell you an RTX 2080 for under $700.

And now we have the announcement of the RTX 2060 with an expected price of $350. I expect the same thing to play out with the GTX 1070 and 1070Ti; bargains in the near term followed by disappearance from the market. If you want a 1070, February is likely to be a good time to buy one, or perhaps March if the 2060 cards are slow to arrive in stores.

comments.text:
Used prices are absolutely awesome right now. I got a Gigabyte Aorus 1080ti (nice premium 1080ti model) 11GB for $400. Was able to give my Strix 1080 to my son. Also found a 1060 6GB for nephew at 130, and a RX580 XFX XXX 8GB for a friend at 100. So hard to recommend new right now with prices being what they are. I got warranty on the 1080ti and 1060, Strix 1080 still under warranty from earlier this year, and all are performing perfectly/quietly/cool. 

RTX seems interesting, but also like it is still sort of in beta. By the time the features are well supported and can run at a high enough framerate @ 4k, we won't be talking about 2070/2080, but more likely about two gens past this one. And that is a big what-if, as it may not actually get off the ground in an a meaningful way, if the compromises are always so severe (eg; penalizing performance to such a degree that someone wanting high resolution + high refresh + max textures has to dial back other things just to turn RTX on sort of makes it useless in the real world). Once we get to zero / negligible performance hit, then it will be ready for prime time.

@RealRaisb  since when is an RTX 2070 a low end card? And if SLI was properly supported, you could have significant performance increases running those 2 cards for a better cost to performance ratio. 

The GTX 970's had great support in SLI,  and I consistently got better benchmarks than when I had a solo GTX 1070, often approaching 1080 levels on games up until 2017, and for less money. 

The performance per dollar ratio is what's important. Even if 2 cards came out to $100 more, if they offered significantly better power than a single card,  that makes it a better investment when the price difference is so small but the performance difference is so large. 

Say some game gets 60 fps with an RTX 2070, and the cost is $600.

Now let's say the same game gets 75 fps with an RTX 2080, and the cost is $800.

That's a $200 difference for 15 fps. Now with the 2070's in SLI, that same game gets 100 fps. The cost is $1200, so $400 more than one 2080, but with a 40 fps increase. That's 1 fps per $10 compared to 1 fps per $13.30 spent with just going with 1 2080.

And that one RTX 2080 ti may just give you 90 fps for $1200, a difference of $600 for 30 fps increase over a solo 2070, but comes out to a loss of $3.33 per frame had you ran 2 x 2070's in SLI.

Again, that's hypothetical since we can't even test it due to not being supported at all, but the point of SLI is to allow further upgrading and enhancing later on, getting results just as good, if not better, than the top cards available.

And what if you could only had $600 to spend, or if you were gifted a 2070? Then a year later you want even more power, would you prefer to only spend $600 more and get better results than a single 2080, or start from scratch and have to spend the full $800-$1200 just to see improvements you could've gotten a lot easier had they only allowed you to SLI?

The highest end cards also stay at their high prices for longer, and go on less. So then SLI becomes even more attractive, like when you see that 1080 ti sitting at $900 yet you could get 2 x  1070's for $750 or less.

comments.text:
bought the gigabyte rtx 2080 gaming oc. It was for $750 and I got a copy of Battlefield V for free (which I was going to buy either way.) so in total I spent ~ $690 on the card. The gtx cards are rising back up in price as people realize that the rtx series isn't as bad as it was at launch. I wouldn't want to risk buying a used GPU anyways. It may be a lot more cheap, but in the end you don't know if it's been damaged at all, modified, a scam listing, or the age of it. Let's say I WERE to buy a 1080 ti for ~$450 used. Chances are pretty high it's been used quite a bit and the lifespan isn't going to be nearly as much as a new card would be. Also unless the seller gives the purchase info, your chances of getting an RMA are zero-to-none. 

The pros of getting an rtx over gtx:
Prices are either the same or around $50-100 for a new graphics card (2070 is a pretty big exception)
better performance overall. If you check the benchmarks for the graphics cards Here: https://www.videocardbenchmark.net/high_end_gpus.html you'll see that even the rtx 2070 (the cheapest and least powerful in the line-up) has surpassed the 1080 ti. Price can be found much lower, and has the dxr (raytracing) functionality
DLSS can give ~25% boost in performance
DXR (raytracing) is a new feature of the rtx lineup.
Future Support will be much better for the rtx series than the gtx series as developers and NVIDIA will work in unison to create games using the rtx features. 

Things to note:
RTX cards and it's features will not be very well optimized as it's brand new tech. 10xx series graphics cards have had years of driver optimizations as well as games being optimized specifically for them which is why you see dxr reducing frames to sub-60 frames (optimized recently to give smooth experience in 1440p with raytracing)

(I'm not ranting about things, I just wanted to share my thoughts and beliefs on the current state of graphics cards.)

Now, here is the math, for the 30% increase in performance that most will not see or notice in a 34" 140 Hz screen with G-Sync. 4K, lol, it's on its way out since 90% of humans cannot see all or most 4 K -- Research it yourselves. So, 30% performance increase with a 70% rise in cost over the GTX 1080ti. Is the new card, the RTX 2080ti really worth it?

The painfully obvious answer is no, no it's not. I paid $669.99 for my PNY GTX 1080ti with 11 GB DDR5  versus some sort of vaporware feature that does not exist in most modern games. Here is something that most people don't even consider. The power consumption of the RTM 2080ti is at the least requires 1/3 more power at near idle than the GTX 1080ti running at 40%. Fan speeds are higher at idle on the RTM along with the redundant higher idle temp. It seems to me that the RTM 2080ti runs hotter even when playing XBox Majong than the GTX 1080ti playing Civilization VI with ultra high settings for 20 minutes. Also, the outright power consumption of the RTM 2080ti is absolutely absurd. I use a very expensive UPS system with all kinds of measuring features to include total watts used for my office equipment to include both the Alienware Area 51 and the Alienware 17xR4 that consumes with everything a grand total of 120 watts coming through the UPS at $0.13 KWH at max performance of benching 100% on both systems. This gives me 25 minutes during a complete power outage for my equipment to shut down safely. However, with the RTM 2080ti, I am down a dismal 12 to 14 minutes with 128 to 130 watts draw measuring on the UPS -- The UPS cannot even give me a stable number as I suspect the RTM Card is unstable all on its lonesome. Yeah, it's that obvious. Now, that is an 8 watts per hour increase in running the POS. Multiply 8 watts x24x365  comes out to an increase of 70080 Watts or 70 KW difference between the GTX1080ti verses the RTM 2080ti and at $0.13 KWH to a total financial increase of $1,138.80 yearly on my electric bill. Yeah so, after paying for the RTM 2080ti, guess what? You're really paying now. Most people pay more per KWH than I currently do. comments.text:
On the bright side, I don't feel too bad about buying a 1080ti just before the announcement of the 2070/2080. Sure it might be a bit cheaper now, but it looks like this next gen isn't offering much in terms of a raw performance boost until software takes advantage of it. That will probably take a few years -
 
This is similar to the story of the original Xbox released against the PS2. The Xbox supposedly had superior graphics capabilities due to the built in directX tools, but games weren't built to take advantage of that for some time, so there was no significant difference in graphics quality on release. Years later games started popping up with bump mapping, advanced shadows & light reflection, etc... to make Xbox the unquestioned winner in terms of graphics (for that generation). 

The problem is, unlike console games, PC game developers do not develop for proprietary hardware; games are expected to run on all high end graphics cards regardless of brand. If Nvidia cards are the only ones with ray tracing, I don't expect any AAA developers to take advantage of that if it means sacrificing functionality on other cards.

comments.text:
Presumably, the 2070 has the same binning system and the 2080 and 2080ti. If so that means the "reference" 2070 is the one on the "lower grade" chip and not permitted to be factory overclocked. If AIB partners are selling at prices closer to the already overclocked "founders edition" cards, then it is likely that they are selling the "higher grade" chips that are permitted to be factory overclocked.
If all of this confusion is correct, then we will eventually get the lower grade chips being sold by AIB partners at closer to MSRP. In fact you may see more of those lower grade chips on sale once AMD release Navi. Especially if at the high end Navi is on par with the RTX2080 just as the RX Vega 64 was in the same bracket as the GTX 1080 and not the GTX 1080ti as countless reviewers started running comparisons of because of the retailer inflated pricing.
I watched Jesen's 2hour presentation and from the very get go reviewers have been confused by the change in strategy by Nvidia regarding their founders edition cards. So they keep referring (in some cases) to the FE cards are reference cards even though they are not. I for one can see why Nvidia did this especially after the crypto excuse for price gouging by retailers last year. So with Nvida selling overclocked cards directly; something I hope AMD eventually start doing too, it means that there is, in theory at least, an upper limit price control. If, I don''t know some store, CanCompParts decides to put an asking price of US$1500 on the ROG RTX 2080 (not the RTX 2080ti), and I can get the, again OVERCLOCKED RTX 2080ti FE card directly from Nvidia, then I will know CanCompParts are price gouging and trying to rip consumers off so I would go directly to Nvidia. This type of shopping around is something reviewers and tech journalists should educating gamers and people buying these cards on rather than simply attacking Nvida on the pricing of the Turing cards. Jensen earlier in the year did say GPU prices weren't going down anytime soon, so this level of pricing should have been expected. 
Basically in what I see as Nvidia's new FE pricing setup, US$50-US$200 (depending on AIB overclock and other customizations) above the OVERCLOCKED Founders Edition card price becomes an upper limit for the pricing of these cutdown Volta GPUs Nvidia named Turing. Only EVGA KINGPIN or custom PCB or water cooled and equivalent RTX 2080ti/2080/2070 GPUs should justify a price mark-up close to the US$200 level.

comments.author: @aland1618

comments.text:
97th percentile = The frame rate was higher than this number 97% of the time. Think of it as the minimum FPS with a buffer to deal with incidental spikes; It's essentially the measure of how smooth the frame rate variation is. A number closer to the average means less variation during gameplay.

So for example, say the average FPS in a game is 100, and the minimum ends up being 25 FPS because there was a hiccup (typically seen as assets stream in from disk). If the 97th percentile ended up at 75 FPS, that means 97% of the time, the FPS was higher than 75, which would better indicate the reality of how much smoother the gameplay really was than the absolute minimum of 25 would.

Does anybody else remember Jensen Huang yelling at Gamescom that RTX 2070 is more powerful than GTX Titan Xp  (https://youtu.be/IG2wVjQUr3c?t=11227) ?  I must say I was pretty stoked back then with the promise of a $500 card that performs on par with, or BETTER than, the $1,200 Titan Xp. 
Tinan Xp is ~5% faster than GTX 1080 Ti or, to make things simple, let's say it's just as fast. But as we see now from LTT's and every other reputable Youtuber's review, the RTX 2070's performance is nowhere near that of GTX 1080 Ti. It's more like a GTX 1080. 
So I am thinking maybe we should all get the 2070 and open a class action lawsuit against nVidia for false advertising? 

On the other hand, it looks like no matter what we do, we, PC gamers/enthusiasts, get the shaft. If it's not the miners driving up GPU prices to the stratosphere, then it's lack of competition. comments.text:
Maybe? off topic.... it's time the fans take a step back and look at team AMD. The Ryzen 2700X is no joke. The Vega 64 is more than capable, and last I checked cost $250 LESS than a 1080TI, much less the RTX stuff. 
I bought Intel/Nvidea hardware going back to Windows 98 days. I spent a year trying to figure how I wanted to build my new rig as my 2009 X58 was obviously getting a tad log in the tooth, starting last fall already.Intel's I7 chip had made it to the next step, and was priced at a really nice price point. Then the insane price spike in GPU's hit.  So I put it off for all of this last summer. Then I read about team AMD's Ryzen chips. 
The more I looked into the Ryzen stuff, the more I liked. So I thought, whatev's, lets check out their GPU's. Low and behold, while widely regarded by the unterelite as inferior, the majority of benchmarks showed the Vega cards were more than capable of running basically everything out there currently at full max. And then of course, there was the price. All that elitist talk of inferiority had allowed the Vega 64 to remain, at least relative to the market, within reach. So I picked up an ASUS ROG Strix unit, full of pretty neon lights etc. 

Intel and AMD are back to the (very) old ways of trying to outdo each other with their CPU's- which is good for consumers- and Nvidea is using this stupid mining price spike as an excuse to price gouge their loyal customers/fans and released their new card IMO timed as it was specifically to ride that wave for extreme profit. Why not hold it for a few months more and allow developers to actually make software to utilize it's features? Because the mining crash was on, prices were starting to slip, and they needed to create a bunch of artificial demand and hype to cash in on the big wave from the price spike. It also allows them to set a precedent that this new $500+ price point should be "normal". It's all win/win for Nvidea, and lose/lose for customers. 

Stop being an Intel/Nvidea fanboi, take a step back and look at how Nvidea is doing business. Look at the actual, realistic performance for what you pay. I went to AMD, for the first time in decades. No regrets. This rig is so fast, stupid Windows 10 is the bottleneck to the whole system. Why pay extra, pay premium, pay price gouging price points for hardware? Is it habit? "Loyalty"? Do you feel you owe it to Nvidea for some reason? Peer pressure? Do what you need to do, but the $$ I saved on my GPU by refusing to be price gouged paid for all my RAM. 

Maybe next year some games will come out that can use the new RTX features. I will worry of it then. Besides, the next AMD card will likely be out by then, and Nvidea will have to up it's game to keep it's "top spot" and maintain it's newfound price gouging business model.

Factorio. The optimization the devs put into this game is amazing but it encourages you to build bigger and bigger and at some point the CPU just can't handle it anymore. Kerbal. I haven't looked into it but I'm not sure if there is a computer that can run this game at 60+ fps when you build a really big rocket. 

Astroneer. This is an early access title and performance issues are a well known problem.

comments.text: Side effect of the death throes of Moore's Law.  If you want more performance, you'll need to pay for it through increased manufacturing costs of larger dies and/or more exotic configurations (multi-chip).  With that S-curve of manufacturing innovation plateauing, you should expect bleeding edge electronics to iteration similar to how mature industries do.  When you buy a newer model of car, if you want a significant bump in performance you're generally looking at having to increase engine displacement and complexity, and you're going to have to pay extra for every bit of that.

The New Sweet Spot for 1440p is now 2070 🤩  It Sits between 1080 & 1080ti in traditional rasterization.  

2070 has Less Cuda Cores & texture units than the 1080( 2304 vs 2560 & 144TU vs 160TU)  yet the 2070 is  faster -till now the gap will increases as drivers will become more optimized , developers get use to the new architecture etc.

Take a look at the  Die Leap : 

2070 (TU 106) :445mm2 , 10.8 billion transistors 

1080(GP 104): 314 mm² , 7.2 billion transistors

With an added advantage of : 

DLSS ( 25 Supported titles till now waiting to be patched only including PUBG , Shadow of the Tomraider , FF 15 ...)   , RT Cores , Tensor Cores , AI , Neural Networks 

HDR Tone Mapping 

Hybrid Rendering 

Dedicated HDR PipeLine to reduce latency with HDR , HDR on Pascal is a real latency mess up since it is SW processed.

GDDR6 (448 GB/s vs 320 GB/s of memory bandwidth on the 1080)

DP 1.4 with DSC 

RT 

It is a definite leap in technology.

HardOCP: 

Is Turing Faster?

With both video cards operating nearly at the same frequency this creates an interesting scenario. We are basically looking at two video cards with similar clock speeds. We can estimate if GeForce RTX 2070’s Turing architecture might be faster than the previous Pascal architecture. It is important to realize there are more SM Units but less CUDA Cores (64 CUDA cores per SM versus 128 on Pascal) and Texture Units on GeForce RTX 2070 when compared to GeForce GTX 1080. In terms of GPU performance, this would mean slower performance on GeForce RTX 2070 if clock speed is the same. However, Turing is a new architecture. There are technically more SM Units, even if there are less CUDA Cores per SM. What we can then gather is if the architectural changes make up for the loss in overall CUDA Cores and Texture Units.
According to our testing the results all signs point to yes, the Turing architecture is definitely superior to, and faster than, the Pascal architecture at similar clock speeds. In all of our testing the MSI GeForce RTX 2070 GAMING Z consistently provided faster performance at 1440p and 4K compared to the MSI GeForce GTX 1080 GAMING X video card, despite having a CUDA Core and Texture Unit deficit, at the same clock speeds. Let’s break it down.

I don't think RTX is going to be a big thing in games any time soon.
It's a feature that is relatively complicated to implement. More than some special ambient occlusion or what other exclusive features nvidia had in the past. What makes it even worse is that they limited it to their high end cards.
For big AAA games whose studios would have the resources to implement RTX the PC already has a much smaller market share than consoles. And on this already limited market it's exclusive to the tiny fraction of people who own a brand new high end graphics card. I don't see many studios investing their resources into that.
It furthermore isn't as big of a deal as Nvidia says. It absolutely destroys performance and the only thing it has to offer is better reflections when screen space reflections do a pretty good job most of the times.
I guess the real reason nvidia put these in is that they want to sell more to people who use this feature for rendering or deep learning. 
Although the second is mostly limited by memory bandwidth for many applications.

comments.text: @hardcoreteunes  The release of RTX isn't up to Nvidia but by the implementation of game devellopers. Since AMD rules the console market and 90% of gamers are on consoles, only game devellopers that don't just create crappy console ports for PC will implement it. The PS3 did have nvidia graphics (though not very capable) so anything they brought to the market back then was part of the PS3 SDK's so if game devellopers deemed a feature usefull, they'd implement it. Ray tracing is an interesting technology that can make games look more realistic but it is a feature for devellopers, not consumers. Because the ray tracing capable hardware has only a tiny market share and devellopment costs are to be earned back at the same time, nvidia markets ray tracing as a feature to consumers to justify the higher price that comes with it. Nvidia must get their ray tracing market share up by leveraging their pc gamer marketshare and hype may boost sales so game devellopers will be interested in implementing ray tracing. Don't forget: The people actually creating a game would really want to use a feature like ray tracing even if it's only for the tiny 0.05% of gamers out there with the compatible hardware for it, but their accountant will never let them.

comments.text:
I think people are "encouraged to skip generations" because raw performance just isn't increasing that much. And it can't. From an architectural standpoint there is just not that much to gain anymore since DirectX and shader model have been conceptually very stable over the last decade. And new process nodes take longer and longer do develop, with the nice cherry on top that 10nm has been a joke compared to 14/16nm (performance gains are basically nonexistent).
But I think that's exactly the reason why nVidia introduced the whole RTX thing. They need a new selling point and a reason for people to upgrade. They can't keep increasing die-sizes to give us more performance. And to be honest, if ray tracing gets adopted by game developers it could be really dope, so let's hope for the best.
But I agree, the first "sensible to buy" RTX card is probably releasing 1-2 years from now and be called RTX 30XX or RTX 21XX.

This basically means the moment a better node than the 12nm one that they are using is viable the 2000 series will die.

For some perspective AMD will be apparently building Vega20 on the 7nm node at TSMC in q4 of this year (that's the next 2 months). Now that is a enterprise card and will come with a enterprise cost so that makes it possible for AMD to do that. So the process node will be there and capable of producing the product but the cost for a consumer card wont be. It's just a question of how long we need to wait.

I don't think RTX 2000 will be long lived.
